# On the Pleasure of Getting Lost

I've been thinking about how rare it is to genuinely not know where you are anymore. GPS has made it nearly impossible—there's always a blue dot showing your exact position, waiting to redirect you back to the intended route.

But there's something valuable about being lost.

When I was younger, my friends and I would ride our bikes into neighborhoods we'd never explored, following nothing but curiosity. We'd discover dead-end streets with interesting architecture, stumble upon small parks nobody talked about, find corner stores with owners who knew everyone by name. The uncertainty was thrilling. Each turn was a choice that mattered because we didn't know what came next.

I'm not arguing against navigation technology—it's obviously useful when you have somewhere to be. But I wonder if we've lost something by making wandering impossible. There's a difference between choosing to explore and choosing to arrive.

Lost-ness used to be an invitation: to pay attention, to talk to strangers, to slow down. It created space for serendipity. Now we optimize every journey, treating getting there as the only point, the experience of traveling merely an inconvenience to minimize.

Maybe the antidote isn't to completely abandon our tools, but to sometimes silence them. To take a wrong turn on purpose. To walk in a direction without knowing what's there. To allow ourselves to be, briefly, truly lost—not desperate or frightened, but genuinely uncertain.

It might remind us that sometimes the journey is the destination after all.
